label: paragraph_title
text: OUR RENTS LAW.

label: text
text: Those who have petitioned H.E. the Governor in behalf of the 7,000 members of the Hongkong Tenants' Protective Association, which represents upwards of 100,000 residents of Hongkong, to suspend the Rents Ordinance permitting an increase of 15 per cent. on the standard rent, seem to have made out a good case. The arguments advanced affect primarily the Chinese community, although one or two might well be used to represent conditions amongst the foreign community. Since the outbreak of the "strike" over 500 distress warrants have been issued for rent in arrear, and, as a result, there is a great deal of empty property. Statistics at the moment of writing are not available, but we may take it for granted that the number of warrants devoted is exceptional and, in the main, due entirely to the unnecessary and harsh conditions forced on the

label: text
text: whether as tenants, owners, mortgage holders,—to say nothing of the Government as rate collectors—are so vitally interested in property.

label: text
text: How often in the last hundred years, in the imagination of men of week knees and little faith, has this country been on the verge of ruin?—Mr. Asquith.

label: text
text: has been made for rent in arrear only in the "strike" months, it seems to reflect hardly on Chinese property owners who have not been moved to grant a sort of moratorium. The looker-on has to remember that property owners generally are liable for rates and Crown Rent, and very often for interest on mortgage: The situation is difficult for all concerned. If the suspension of the 15 per cent, order is likely to make a change for the good, public opinion will fervently hope that H.E. the Governor will listen favourably to the petition. The petitioners are decided in their opinion that Chinese tenants affected by the Rents Ordinance cannot afford to pay an increase of rent above Standard Rent until the trade conditions within the Colony resume a normal state. The alternative to a suspension seems to be simply one of overcrowding into other premises, to create a spirit of discontentment, to convey a wrong impression to the evil-doers at Canton, and to put the Colony's administration into a bad light. A suspension of the Ordinance giving the powers referred to should do some good. Property owners should be glad of postponement which at once cancels the main argument for the non-payment of rent, and strengthens their hands in seeking lawful demands. Tenants will be encouraged to meet their contracts, and the spirit of unrest will be killed at its birth. The signatories to the petition state that the great majority of the proprietors of small businesses and shops, and wage earners, are permanent residents and are law abiding and peaceful persons. Recent events seem to bear out the latter part of this contention. Police patrols were, in the main, singularly free from the capture of many undesirables, whilst a feature of the work of the cordons was the relatively small numbers of unwanteds they caught when compared with the total population of either the districts concerned or the Colony as a whole. label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE.

label: text
text: (To the Editor of the China Mail).

label: text
text: Sir,—I crave for a little space within your columns to express my appreciation for one whose untimely death has cast a gloom over the entire Colony. It has been my privilege and fortune to have known the late Mr. Ho Cheuk intimately for well night twenty years, as a promising youth, as a devoted husband and as an affectionate father.

label: text
text: Genial in disposition, he had always a good word for someone; quiet by nature, most of his many good deeds were done quietly; unassuming in manner, he was "tender towards the bashful, gentle towards the distant and merciful towards the absurd."

label: text
text: A devoted husband, he never returned home without a parcel or something for his wife. A tender father he spared no pains to inspire his children with the highest and taught them the best. A filial son, he loved his father and mother dearly. An ideal brother, he was ideal to the end: A helpful neighbour, he was always a friend in need. Since the beginning of the strike right up to a week before his regrettable end, he was up early every day to get ice and food and attend to the needs of his neighbours. Throughout his short but serviceable life he had no enemies while the record attendance at his funeral amply justifies the highest esteem in which he was (and still is) held.

label: text
text: In expressing my deepest sympathy to those who are his dearest and nearest, let me also mention that though it seemed cruel that such a promising life should be abruptly end, yet heaven hath endowed us with his spirit which will never die but will always be present to inspire his friends to a nobler living and his loved ones to a more perfect trust in the goodness and mercy of Providence.

PARKING AND EPSTEIN.
An idea is none the less effective for being simple. In our salad days

label: text
text: and when our favourite circus came to town, the life was wont to be crushed out of us almost by the surging crowds that attempted to concentrate on the narrow opening leading to the pay-box. It helped a little when the funny man in the crowd shouted—"Mind me eggs." Then someone invented the queue and other was evolved out of chaos. Someone has thought of a very good idea in relation to the official stands for motor cars in Pedder Street and opposite the Post Office. The new arrangement allows more cars to be parked and in that sense is a good idea. Those who rhapsodise on cylinders and “-miles to the gallon” will probably resent the suggestion that a serried row of old and new motor cars is not exactly a joy for ever... Perhaps a local Epstein will arise and design a motor "sanctuary." If it will be on the lines of his Hudson memorial—in that it will give rise to discussion on form and beauty—some good will result. We take the offerings of our architects without protest. Many of them are like the British Premier who admits he has no imagination. This explains everything: It may even explain the reason for a non-reply to that $700 cable.... But there are exceptions. Surely a word of praise is due to the Government official who designed the entrance to the Prince's Pier. Here is form that compels attention. It is in keeping with the exquisite Cenotaph close by. We enter its openings and feel we are about to gain admittance to a Roman Stadium. If the same conscious thought that seems to have been given to this design, can be transferred to other building projects, there will be no need to emphasise Mr. Bernard Shaw's opinion that all buildings should be razed after an existence of ten years. Perhaps the Government will take the trouble of adding a few Epsteins to its P.W.D. staff. They would prove good investments.

text: One Way. Guardian's' correspondent sends an interesting story from China:—

label: text
text: A common newspaper essay since the troubles started has been on the subject: "Why I believe in war with Great Britain." In one of the most recent of these. disquisitions, written in a purely academic style, a well-known scholar points out how easily China could annihilate the entire British fleet by decoying all our bluejackets from their ships into the interior and then murdering them at leisure. The captors would then proceed leisurely back to the coast, take possession of the ships, and sail for London, reducing the British capital with British naval guns.

A SUBSIDISED THEATRE.
Are any of us likely to live to see a Hongkong Governor intro-

label: text
text: duce a budget which shall have some such item as this:—

label: text
text: Under Educational and Artists objects: To grant a sum of $1,000 to the Hongkong A.D.C. to encourage it in its effort to produce Classical and Shakespearean plays." It would be money well spent. The suggestion is prompted by the news that the Irish Free State has voted $14,500 toward the endowment of a national theatre. Part is to go to the directors of the Abbey Theatre for the production of plays on Irish subjects written in English, and part to the Irish-speaking dramatic society, An Comhar Dramiochta, for plays in Irish. This is the first time a State subsidy for the encouragement of the drama has ever been granted in Great Britain or Ireland, and it is hailed as another gratifying outcome of the autonomous powers conferred on the Free State by the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The endowment probably will be enlarged in future years if the results justify such a course. The grant to the Abbey Theatre will be specially useful in enabling it not only to make larger payment to authors but also to retain promising actors and actresses against the inducements offered to them by British and American managers. An Comhar Dramiochta, which came into being a couple of years ago, also produces its plays at the Abbey Theatre, but is managed separately. Already it has presented a number of quite excellent plays and the company, which is composed exclusively of amateurs, includes several actors of decided ability. The audiences are steadily increasing, and high hopes are entertained for the movement, particularly in view of the intensive teaching of the Irish language now in progress in all the public schools.

label: paragraph_title
text: HUSBANDS AND WIVES.

label: text
text: The female box, said the great Blackstone, is "a great favourite of the laws of England." The odd thing is that women have never been able to see it, remarks a Home paper. For generations they have been demanding emancipation, and getting it, till only small portions of their old privileges remain to them. For half a century wives have been allowed to look after their own property and get rid of it, as they please. Within our own time they have, to the ill-concealed delight of the malicious male, insisted on coming into the jury-box. In general, women, even though they be wives, now have to pay up like men. Such are the joys of equality. But the equality was still imperfect. That illogical state of the law deplored by Mr. Bumbler still obtains: "The law opposes," said Mr. Brownlow, "that your wife acts under your direction." "If the law supposes that," said Mr. Bumble; the law is a ass-a idiot. If that's the eye of the law, the law is a bachelor, and the worst I wish the law is, that his eye may be opened by experience." Distinguished jurists in our time have declared their opinion that the law in this matter is an abschronian. It is absurd, they pronounce, to suppose that a woman who has the same right as her husband to acquire and administer property to vote in Parliament may elect to hold any

label: text
text: husband's knowledge cannot be punished, but must be assumed to have been his tool, is denounced by the very judges who have to act upon it. There can indeed be little doubt that from time to time it has procured the acquittal of the active partner and the punishment of the weaker or actually innocent member of the firm. But whatever the state of the law juries, and judges too, will be reluctant to make the wife equally responsible with the husband for a crime in which both were concerned. Crimes, however, are not the only offences with which the Courts are occupied. There are also such things as torts, injuries done to the individual as distinct from injuries done to the community which are breaches of the law. The Lord Chancellor has now introduced a bill to provide that no husband shall have to pay for the torts committed by his wife. Thus another of the rights of women will at length be won. Whether she did the deed before or after marriage, it is she who will have to pay for it hence forth and the injured party will not get a penny out of the husband. Such at least is to be the law of the matter. But we have no confidence in these husbands. They are a feeble to be. Most of them, we see no shadow of doubt, will pay up rather than rely on their legal defence, will pay anything in reason rather than let their offend in.
